lesson_title: Iron Fire: From Clay Furnace to Blast Furnace
hook_text: African smiths were making iron here more than a thousand years ago, with clay, charcoal and goatskin bellows.
clip_script: Iron ore isn't iron. It is iron locked up with oxygen. To set the metal free, you need carbon and serious heat. Over a thousand years ago, smiths in southern Africa built clay furnaces, packed them with charcoal and crushed ore, and pumped goatskin bellows for hours until the fire roared. The charcoal stole the oxygen, leaving a spongy lump of iron that they hammered into hoes and spears. Today a blast furnace does the same chemistry on a giant scale: coke makes carbon monoxide, and Fe2O3 plus 3CO gives 2Fe plus 3CO2. Limestone drags out the rubbish as slag. Then blow pure oxygen through the iron to burn off extra carbon, and brittle iron becomes strong steel.
visual_style: Firelit reconstruction of a clay furnace with bellows; molten iron pouring from a blast furnace; the balanced equation sliding together atom by atom.
pacing: A bold heritage open, a rhythmic bellows build, a fast cut to the modern furnace, a crisp steel finish.
